Dirge

DURJ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Dirge is a mournful song or hymn expressing grief, especially for the dead.

The bagpiper's slow dirge drifted across the cemetery as the procession made its way to the gravesite.

Worked Example

Instead of the usual celebratory anthem, the marching band played a somber dirge in memory of the coach who had passed away that summer.

A dirge is specifically a piece of music or poetry meant to mourn -- not just any slow or sad song.

Antonyms

How Strong Is It? — ballad → dirge → wail

ballad vs. dirge

ballad vs. dirge: A ballad can tell any story, sad or happy, set to music -- with no requirement to mourn.

wail vs. dirge

wail vs. dirge: A person's raw, spontaneous wail of grief is more intense and unstructured than a composed dirge.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — dirige

root — dirige: direct! (the opening word of a funeral chant, "Direct, O Lord...") (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Dirge is a shortened form of Latin dirige ("direct!"), the first word of a medieval funeral chant -- the whole ceremony's name shrank down to describe any mournful funeral song.

Where it comes from

Where it comes from: Medieval funeral chants opened with the Latin command 'Dirige' -- 'Direct, O Lord...' -- and English clipped that single opening word into the name for the whole mournful song. It is a word named by its first word, the way some hymns are known by their opening line.

Word Choice

A dirge is a piece of music or verse specifically composed to mourn -- you might also hear the related term elegy for a similar piece of serious, reflective mourning, which this course covers as its own word.
